extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and moral/political theory (readers of Hobbes)
extracted.subtask_description: A section of Hobbes' Leviathan that defines science, reason, passions, and intellectual virtues and gives prescriptive criteria for clear reasoning, classification of passions, and evaluative distinctions for discourse and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perspicuous words; avoid metaphors in truth-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: In reckoning and seeking of truth, metaphoric or ambiguous speech (e.g., 'The Way Goeth', 'The Proverb Sayes') is not to be admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Light of humane minds is Perspicuous Words, but by exact definitions first snuffed, and purged from ambiguity; Metaphors, and senslesse and ambiguous words, are like Ignes Fatui, and reasoning upon them, is wandering amongst innumerable absurdities; their end, contention, and sedition, or contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid names that signify nothing (canting scholastic terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from using learned, rote names that signify nothing (examples: 'Hypostatical, Transubstantiate, Consubstantiate, Eternal-now').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such canting of School-men are names learned by rote and not to be admitted in seeking truth; they contribute to ambiguity and absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Science: naming + orderly method
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is attained by apt imposing of Names and by getting a good and orderly Method in proceeding from the Elements (names) to Assertions, to Syllogismes, yielding knowledge of all consequences of names pertaining to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science differs from Sense and Memory (knowledge of fact); Science is knowledge of consequences and dependence, enabling one to reproduce effects when causes come into one's power; thus scientific discourse must start with exact definitions and proceed by connexions to demonstrable conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Prudence (experience) from Sapience (science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence arises from experience (natural dexterity and memory), whereas Sapience arises from much science; the Latins distinguished Prudentia (experience) from Sapientia (science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a skilled swordsman without science has prudence; one with science of possible offences/guards has sapience and is more infallible. Do not equate experience-based knack with methodical scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural prudence to reliance on false general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of causes is less harmful than relying on false rules; forsaking natural judgement to follow general sentences read in authors is a sign of folly (Pedantry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In business without infallible science, one should not abandon one's own natural judgement for general dicta of authors who are subject to exceptions; trust experience over spurious general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science: certain (teachable demonstration) vs uncertain (particular confirmations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of science are either certain—when the claimant can teach and demonstrate the truth perspicuously to another—or uncertain—when only some particular events answer to the pretence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of prudence are all uncertain (experience-based). For an asserted science, the strongest evidence is the ability to demonstrate and teach the principles clearly; repeated empirical successes are weaker/uncertain signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of speech correspond to passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different passions are customarily expressed by different grammatical/forms of speech: Deliberation by the Subjunctive; Desire/Aversion by the Imperative (becoming Command, Prayer, or Counsel); Desire-to-know by the Interrogative; Vaine-glory/Indignation/Pity/Revengfulness by the Optative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are not certain signs of passion (they can be used arbitrarily), but are the conventional voluntary expressions. Best signs of present passion remain countenance, bodily motions, actions, and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral terms (good/evil) are relative to the agent or sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: What any man desires (appetite) he calls good; what he hates (aversion) he calls evil. There is nothing simply and absolutely good or evil; common rules of good/evil derive from the person's viewpoint, the person representing the commonwealth, or a judge agreed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions or objects, recognise that 'good' and 'evil' are relational terms tied to appetite/aversion and social authority; avoid assuming absolute moral properties in objects themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish three senses of good/evil (promise, effect, means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good has three kinds: Good in the Promise (Pulchrum), Good in Effect (Jucundum, Delightful), and Good as the Means (Utile, Profitable); likewise for evil: Turpe (promise), Molestum (effect), Inutile (means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing things, separate whether they promise good, actually produce delight/effect, or serve as useful means; use appropriate terms to avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pleasures of sense from pleasures of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures arising from immediate sense-contact are 'Pleasures of Sense'; pleasures arising from expectation or foresight of ends are 'Pleasures of the Mind' (Joy). Displeasures analogously divide into Pain (sense) and Grief (expectation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when analyzing motivations and evaluating actions: some delights are bodily and immediate whereas others are intellectual/anticipatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of passions and their defining relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are defined as motions/endeavours of the heart: Appetite/Desire (toward), Aversion (from), Love/ Hate (same concepts with presence/absence nuance). Compound passions are defined by combinations with opinion: Hope (appetite + opinion of attaining), Despair (appetite without opinion), Fear (aversion + opinion of hurt), Courage (aversion + hope of avoiding hurt), Anger (sudden courage), Confidence (constant hope), Diffidence (constant despair), Indignation (anger for injury to another), Benevolence (desire of good to another), Covetousness, Ambition, Pusillanimity, Magnanimity, Valour, Liberality, Miserablenesse/Parsimony, Kindness, Natural Lust, Luxury, Passion of Love/Jealousy, Revengefulness, Curiosity, Religion/Superstition, Panique Terror, Admiration, Glory/Vaine-glory, Dejection, Sudden Glory (Laughter), Sudden Dejection (Weeping), Shame/Blushing, Impudence, Pity/Compassion, Cruelty, Emulation/Envy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions tie each passion to combinations of appetite/aversion and opinions about consequences or presence/absence. Use this taxonomy to identify motivations and predict related facial/body signs and typical verbal expressions; note also how customs/culture and age affect prevalence (e.g., vainglory common in youth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and the Will: procedural definition of volition
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation is the alternating succession of appetites, aversions, hopes and fears about the same thing, considered until action or impossibility. The Will is the last appetite or aversion adhering immediately to the action or omission—the act (not the faculty) of willing. A voluntary act is one that proceeds from the Will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For assessment of voluntariness, identify the final inclination immediately before action; earlier inclinations that did not immediately adhere to the action do not make an action voluntary. Both appetites toward and aversions from may be sources of voluntary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual virtues: wit, judgement, discretion; natural vs acquired
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual virtues are valued abilities of mind: 'Natural Witte' (celerity of imagination and steady direction), 'Good Wit'/'Fancy' (ability to find rare similitudes), 'Good Judgement' (discernment of differences, difficult distinguishing), and 'Discretion' (judgement of times, places, persons). Natural wit arises from use/experience without method; acquired virtues require method and steady application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem requires more fancy (extravagancy) but must avoid indiscretion; a good history requires eminent judgement (method, truth, and choice of profitable actions). Excessive fancy without steadiness leads to digressions; cultivate both judgement and steady direction toward ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative forms of speech: praise, magnification, felicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of speech signifying opinion of goodness is 'PRAISE'; for power/greatness, 'MAGNIFYING'; felicity (continuous success in obtaining desires) is the notion of human felicity in this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating evaluation, use these genres of speech appropriately; remember felicity of this life is continual success in obtaining desires but is not perpetual tranquillity—life intrinsically involves motion and desire.
